# Smuggling Under Prohibition: Concealment Methods in Vehicles

When the Eighteenth Amendment took effect in 1920, it created an enormous black market for alcohol, and smugglers—known as "rum-runners" and "bootleggers"—developed increasingly sophisticated ways to hide liquor in vehicles while transporting it past federal Prohibition agents and border patrols.

## False Compartments and Hidden Spaces

The most iconic technique was the false compartment. Bootleggers built hidden cavities into car bodies, under floorboards, behind seat panels, inside door frames, and beneath running boards. These "traps" were often operated by hidden levers or springs so that a casual inspection revealed nothing. Skilled craftsmen—some former coachbuilders or carpenters—became sought-after specialists who could make a compartment virtually undetectable. Some cars were so well built that agents needed to dismantle the vehicle to find the cargo.

## Oversized and Modified Fuel Tanks

Liquor was frequently carried in enlarged or double-walled gas tanks, with alcohol stored in a sealed inner chamber surrounded by fuel. A probe dropped into the tank would hit gasoline, satisfying a suspicious officer. The downside was real: a crash or a spark could be catastrophic, and drivers sometimes had to drain fuel to reach the cargo.

## Bulk and Weight Concealment

Larger shipments moved in trucks with false loads. Smugglers hid bottles under legitimate cargo—hay, produce, ice, lumber—or inside hollowed-out loads of bricks and cement blocks. Some trucks carried casks suspended beneath the chassis in fabricated undercarriages, and others used false walls that extended cargo beds by several feet. Ice trucks were especially useful, since melting ice explained dripping water and the cold masked the smell of alcohol.

## The Sea and the Handoff

Much liquor arrived by sea—"rum rows" of ships anchored just beyond U.S. territorial waters (initially three miles, later extended to twelve) off the Atlantic coast. Small, fast boats ferried cases ashore at night, transferring cargo to waiting automobiles on secluded beaches. Coastal roads became gauntlets of checkpoints, which pushed smugglers toward speed as a strategy.

## Speed as a Concealment Strategy

Concealment alone wasn't always enough, so smugglers modified engines. The most famous example is the "Whiskey Petes" tradition: stripped-down, supercharged Fords and other hot rods built to outrun agents. These vehicles—ancestors of stock car racing and NASCAR—often carried little or no concealment at all, relying instead on horsepower. Some drivers added armored plating and, in extreme cases, mounted machine guns.

## Detection and Countermeasures

Customs officers developed countermeasures: probing tanks with rods, using mirrors on poles to inspect undercarriages, weighing vehicles, and training dogs to detect alcohol. This cat-and-mouse dynamic drove continuous innovation on both sides, making vehicle concealment during Prohibition a genuine chapter in the history of automotive engineering—and, ultimately, of American motorsport.

## Summary

Prohibition-era smugglers combined craftsmanship (false compartments, modified tanks), deception (legitimate-looking loads), and performance (souped-up engines) to move illegal alcohol. Their methods reflected a broader pattern: when law creates a lucrative black market, ingenuity follows the money.
